metadata.title: Using convolutional neural networks to automatically score eight TIMSS 2019 graphical response items

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical response items (restricted-use items included) and constructs image arrays from student screenshots collected during the computer-based administration. The paper reports sample sizes in terms of total responses per item and grade and uses stratified random splits by country and score category for training/validation, but it does not report the use of TIMSS complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures. Because the modeling is performed with CNNs in Keras (and the paper does not describe weight-aware training), the analysis appears to treat the response-level dataset as an unweighted ML sample. The main preprocessing steps are image resizing, greyscaling, contrast/saturation enhancement, pixelation, and (for the trichotomous item) data augmentation to increase partial-credit representation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper uses TIMSS plausible values indirectly via IRT-based expected scores (ES) computed from TIMSS 2019 scaling item parameters and student proficiency estimates, but it does not document a formal missing-data strategy for the underlying student/context data used to compute those proficiency estimates. It also does not report whether any missingness in the image-response dataset or associated metadata was handled via deletion or imputation. This is a reporting gap because missingness handling can affect the construction of ES and therefore the training/validation splits used for CNN cleaning and final scoring.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study identifies all TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical response items, then applies item-selection filters: it excludes one Grade 8 “Building” PSI item already modeled in von Davier et al. (2022) and excludes one item at each grade due to being at the lowest complexity end already covered by secured/restricted-use items. It selects eight items total: five Grade 4 items (Measurement/Geometry) and three Grade 8 Geometry items, including two restricted-use items (ME52048, ME62300). For each item, it uses responses from countries that participated in eTIMSS in the 2019 cycle, then constructs image arrays from student screenshots and human rater classifications. For modeling, it performs stratified hold-out splits by country and score category, uses cross-validation in the final stage (five repeated assignment processes), and removes responses that are identified (via manual review) as incorrectly or inconsistently scored by human raters. For the trichotomous item ME62300, it applies augmentation by duplicating/rotating/mirroring responses to increase partial-credit representation in the final training sample.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 4 Mathematics (Measurement/Geometry graphical response items)
main_findings.target_variable: Graphical response score category (CNN vs human rater; dichotomous items)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best CNNs (across dichotomous items) achieved average accuracy 99.37%–99.92% and F1-scores between 0.9948 and 0.9992; average loss ranged from 0.0063 to 0.0298 on the clean validation samples (Table 8). On incorrectly human-scored responses, CNNs achieved 94.78%–99.60% correct classification into the correct score category (Table 9).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 4 Mathematics graphical response item the study leveraged convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to predict the dichotomous score category of student graphical responses as classified by human raters, finding that the best CNNs achieved near-ceiling agreement (average accuracy ~99.37%–99.92% and F1 ~0.9948–0.9992) and also correctly reclassified most responses that humans had scored incorrectly. This indicates that CNN-based automated scoring can serve as a highly reliable second scoring channel for graphical constructed-response items, potentially reducing rater fatigue and improving scoring consistency in ILSAs.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 8 Mathematics (Geometry graphical response items)
main_findings.target_variable: Graphical response score category (CNN vs human rater; dichotomous items)
main_findings.performance_metrics: For Grade 8 dichotomous items, best CNNs achieved average accuracy 99.89%–99.92% with F1-scores around 0.9991–0.9992 (Table 8). On incorrectly human-scored responses, CNNs achieved 95.15%–99.60% correct classification into the correct score category (Table 9).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 8 Mathematics graphical response item the study leveraged convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to predict dichotomous score categories for student drawings relative to human rater classifications, finding that performance remained extremely high (average accuracy ~99.89%–99.92% and F1 ~0.9991–0.9992). This indicates that CNN-based validation can generalize across grade levels and item types within TIMSS graphical response tasks, supporting operational adoption for second-set scoring and error flagging.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 8 Mathematics (Geometry graphical response item ME62300; trichotomous scoring)
main_findings.target_variable: Graphical response score category (CNN vs human rater; trichotomous items)
main_findings.performance_metrics: For the trichotomous item ME62300, the best CNNs achieved average accuracy 97.99% and average F1-score 0.9766 on the clean validation samples (Table 8). On incorrectly human-scored responses, CNNs achieved 88.81% correct classification into the correct score category (Table 9).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 8 Mathematics data for the trichotomous graphical response item ME62300, the study leveraged convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to predict the three score categories used by human raters, finding that performance remained high but lower than dichotomous items (average accuracy ~97.99% and F1 ~0.9766). This indicates that CNN-based automated scoring is feasible for more complex graphical scoring schemes, but additional attention to partial-credit representation and validation review is needed to maintain reliability.

data.outcome_summary: This study evaluates whether convolutional neural networks can automatically score TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical constructed-response items by classifying student drawings into the same score categories as human raters. The authors selected eight graphical items (five Grade 4 and three Grade 8, including one trichotomous item ME62300) and built image arrays from student screenshots, applying greyscaling, contrast/saturation enhancement, resizing, and pixelation; for ME62300 they also used augmentation to increase partial-credit representation. CNNs were trained and validated using stratified hold-out splits by country and score category, with cross-validation in the final stage. On clean validation samples, dichotomous items reached average accuracy about 99.37%–99.92% with F1 between 0.9948 and 0.9992, while the trichotomous item achieved ~97.99% accuracy and F1=0.9766. The paper reports that CNNs can reclassify most responses that humans scored incorrectly, supporting operational “second-set” scoring, though it does not document a missing-data strategy for the ES/IRT components and does not report survey-weight usage.
